1.text:
Where Are We in the Universe?

Welcome to page one of a year-long trip. It starts with one question: where, exactly, are we? You know your street and your town. This year we keep zooming out, from Earth to the Solar System, then to the Sun and the stars, the galaxy, the whole universe, and finally the question of whether anything lives out there.

Look at the Sun and Earth on this page. The distance between them gets its own name: 1 astronomical unit, or 1 AU. Light is the fastest thing there is, and it still needs about 8.3 minutes to cover that gap. So the sunlight on your face right now left the Sun more than 8 minutes ago, about as long as it takes you to brush your teeth and get dressed.

Before you turn the page, give yourself a quiet half minute. Where do you think we are in the universe?

Did you know? When you look at the Sun (never directly, please!), you are seeing it as it was about 8 minutes ago.

2.text:
If the Sun Were a Grapefruit...

Let's shrink everything. Picture the Sun as a grapefruit about 14 cm across, sitting on your desk. Everything else in space shrinks by the same amount.

Now the question: on that scale, how far away is the next star? Across the room? Across town? Across the country?

Pick an answer and commit to it before you read on. No peeking. We'll find out in the Scale Walk activity later in this deck, and plenty of people guess way off.

3.text:
Today I Can...

Here's what you'll be able to do by the end of this deck. Copy these into your notebook as "I can" statements so you can check yourself at the end.

I can describe Earth's cosmic address. I can measure space with AU and light-years. I can read light, using spectra and Doppler shifts. I can use gravity to explain orbits. And I can explain how new data changed our model of the solar system.

That's a full plate for one lesson. Keep the list handy, because you'll rate yourself on each one when we finish.

4.text:
Part 1: How Big Is It Out There?

Think about the longest trip you've ever taken. Maybe a few hours in a car, or a flight across an ocean. Now imagine measuring something a million times longer than that. Miles and kilometers start to feel like measuring a highway with a ruler.

Astronomers run into that problem every day. In this part, we'll go from our planet out to the edge of what we can see. Along the way you'll build Earth's "cosmic address" and pick up the rulers astronomers use when kilometers just won't cut it.

5.text:
Our Cosmic Address

Your cosmic address works like a set of Russian dolls, each one fitting inside a bigger one. Start with Earth. Earth belongs to the Solar System, which is our Sun and everything that orbits it.

Next comes a level of star groupings: star clusters and multi-star systems. Multi-star systems are two or more stars orbiting each other, and clusters are crowds of stars born together. Here's the catch: our Sun is a single star today and isn't in a cluster, so this layer is a step on the size ladder but not a line in our own address.

Zoom out again and you reach the Milky Way, a galaxy of more than 100 billion stars. The Milky Way is one of the galaxies in the Local Group, which sits inside the Laniakea Supercluster, which is one of countless superclusters in the observable universe. And this drawing is not to scale. Each jump is far bigger than the one before it.

Did you know? Nearly half of Sun-like stars have at least one companion star, so flying solo like our Sun is only one way to be a star.

6.text:
The Astronomical Unit

The AU is the average distance from Earth to the Sun: 1 AU = 1.496 × 108 km, or about 150 million km. Light takes about 8.3 minutes to cross it.

Why "average"? Earth's orbit is very slightly stretched, so our distance from the Sun changes a little over the year. The AU gives us one handy number to work with.

Inside the solar system, the AU is the right ruler for the job. Saying Jupiter is about 5 AU from the Sun and Neptune about 30 AU beats juggling billions of kilometers. As the slide says, this picture is not to scale. If it were, Earth would be a dot too tiny to see.

Did you know? You can check the 8.3 minutes yourself: 150 million km divided by light's speed of 300,000 km per second gives about 500 seconds.

7.text:
The Light-Year

A light-year is how far light travels in one year. It sounds like a time, but it's a distance! One light-year is about 9.46 × 1012 km, close to 10 trillion kilometers.

Light takes time to reach us, and that has an odd side effect: looking far away means looking back in time. Take the Andromeda Galaxy. The light you'd see from it tonight left Andromeda about 2.5 million years ago, before our species even existed. Every picture of a faraway galaxy is an old postcard that took a very long time in the mail.

Did you know? The Milky Way is roughly 100,000 light-years across, so light needs about 100,000 years to cross our own galaxy.

8.text:
Powers of Ten

To compare sizes this far apart, astronomers use powers of ten. Each step up the ladder makes things ten times bigger, and scientific notation lets you write huge numbers without a wall of zeros.

Climb the ladder with the slide: Earth, then Earth to the Sun (1 AU), then the Sun to Neptune, then the Sun to the nearest star, then the Milky Way, and finally the observable universe. At the top, the observable universe is about 1024 km across. That's a 1 with 24 zeros after it.

Try a few estimates as you go. Earth is roughly 104 km wide, and 1 AU is roughly 108 km. That means about 10,000 Earths could line up between us and the Sun (the exact count is closer to 12,000).

Did you know? The observable universe is wider than you might guess from its age, because space kept stretching while the oldest light was traveling toward us.

9.text:
Angular Size

Angular size is how much of the sky an object seems to cover, measured as an angle. The Sun and the Moon both cover about half a degree.

That's a lucky match. The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, but it's also about 400 times farther away, so the two look almost exactly the same size from where you stand. This picture isn't to scale either; the real Sun would be off the page by a long way.

You can measure angles with your own hand. Stretch your arm out: your pinky covers about 1 degree, your fist about 10 degrees. Next time the Moon is up, try covering it with your pinky. It's smaller than it looks.

Did you know? The Sun and Moon looking the same size is why total solar eclipses are possible: the Moon can just barely cover the Sun's bright face.

10.text:
Check for Understanding: Rank by Size

Time to put your cosmic address to work. Here are three things: a galaxy, the Local Group, and the Solar System.

Rank them from smallest to largest: 1, 2, 3. Think back to the Russian dolls on Slide 5. Which doll fits inside which? Write down your order before you move on.

11.text:
Part 2: Light and Spectra

Here's a puzzle. The stars are so far away that we will probably never visit them. So how do we know anything about them at all?

The answer is light. For almost everything in the universe, light is the only messenger that makes it here. Think about how much you can learn about someone from one photo: what they look like, maybe where they were. In this part you'll see that starlight carries a lot more than that, once you know how to read it.

12.text:
Light Is a Wave

Light is a wave, and every light wave follows a simple rule: c = λf. Here c is the speed of light, λ (lambda) is the wavelength, and f is the frequency. Since c never changes, a longer wavelength means a lower frequency, and a shorter wavelength means a higher frequency.

The full family of light is called the electromagnetic spectrum: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, UV, X-ray, and gamma. Going from radio toward gamma, the waves get shorter and carry more energy. The rainbow your eyes can see is one thin slice of the whole thing.

Different light needs different telescopes. Visible light and radio waves pass through our air, so regular telescopes and radio dishes can sit on the ground. JWST studies infrared, Chandra studies X-rays, and Fermi studies gamma rays, all from space, because our atmosphere blocks most of that light before it reaches the ground.

Did you know? Radio waves are light too, not sound. Sound needs air to travel, so it can't cross empty space, but light can.

13.text:
Spectra: Fingerprints in Light

Spread light out into its colors and you get a spectrum. Spectral lines are each element's fingerprint in light. No two elements make the same pattern.

There are three kinds of spectra. A continuous spectrum is a smooth rainbow, made by something hot and dense, like a glowing stove coil. An emission spectrum is mostly dark with a few bright lines, made by a hot, thin gas. An absorption spectrum is a rainbow with dark lines cut out, made when cooler gas sits in front of a hotter glowing source.

Here's the useful part: an element's bright emission lines and its dark absorption lines land in the same spots. Starlight shows absorption lines, so by reading them we can tell what a star is made of without ever getting close to it.

Did you know? The lines happen because electrons in atoms can only sit at certain energy levels, like steps on a staircase, and each jump gives off or soaks up one exact color.

14.text:
The Doppler Shift

You've heard this effect even if you didn't know its name. An ambulance siren sounds higher as it races toward you and lower as it speeds away. Light does the same thing.

Redshift means the source is moving away, so its light gets stretched to longer wavelengths. Blueshift means the source is moving toward us, so its light gets squeezed to shorter wavelengths. As a star moves, the light ahead of it bunches up and the light behind it stretches out.

One catch: a redshifted star doesn't actually look red. Its spectral lines just slide a tiny bit toward the red end. Measuring that slide tells astronomers how fast the object is moving toward or away from us.

Did you know? Almost all galaxies beyond our Local Group are redshifted, which became a key clue that the universe is expanding. You'll dig into that later in the course.

15.text:
Check for Understanding: What Is the Galaxy Doing?

Here's a puzzle real astronomers solve. A galaxy's hydrogen lines show up at longer wavelengths than they do in the lab. What does that tell you?

Is the galaxy A) moving toward us, B) moving away from us, C) hotter than the Sun, or D) made of different elements? Look back at Slides 13 and 14, choose one, and be ready to explain why the other three don't fit.

16.text:
Part 3: Gravity and Orbits

The Moon is always falling toward Earth. So why doesn't it crash into us? And if it's moving so fast, why doesn't it fly off into space?

Here's a warm-up: is there gravity on the International Space Station? Decide what you think now and hang on to it. In this part, gravity turns out to be the force behind a lot, from a falling apple to a spinning galaxy.

17.text:
Universal Gravitation

Gravity means every mass attracts every other mass. You, your pencil, the Moon, and a faraway galaxy are all pulling on one another. Isaac Newton wrote this as a law: Fg = G m1m2 / d2, where G = 6.67 × 10-11 N·m2/kg2.

The formula says two things. Bigger masses pull harder. And distance matters a lot, because this is an inverse-square law. If you go from distance d to distance 2d, the force drops to ¼ Fg. Triple the distance and it falls to one ninth.

That tiny value of G is why you don't feel your desk pulling on you. It takes something the size of a planet to make gravity you can notice.

Did you know? Gravity never fully switches off. It gets weaker with distance, but it never reaches zero.

18.text:
Why Do Astronauts Float?

An orbit means falling around Earth and always missing it. The ISS flies about 400 km up, and about 90% of surface gravity is still pulling on it. So "no gravity in space" is a myth.

The trick is sideways speed. The station moves sideways so fast that as it falls toward Earth, the curved ground drops away beneath it. It keeps falling and keeps missing. The astronauts inside are falling right along with the station, so they float, like riders who lift off their seats as a roller coaster plunges down a big drop.

Newton pictured this with a cannon on a very tall mountain. Fire a ball gently and it lands nearby. Fire it faster and it lands farther away. Fire it fast enough and it never lands at all.

Did you know? The ISS travels around 28,000 km per hour and circles the whole Earth in about an hour and a half.

19.text:
Kepler's Laws

Johannes Kepler worked out how planets move by studying very careful sky measurements made by Tycho Brahe. His first law: orbits are ellipses, slightly stretched circles, with the Sun at one focus (not in the center).

His second law: a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. A planet moves fast near the Sun (at perihelion) and slow when it's far away (at aphelion), so a short, fat wedge and a long, thin wedge cover the same area in the same time.

His third law: farther planets take longer to go around. In numbers, P2 = a3, where P is the period in years and a is the distance in AU. Later, Newton showed that all three of Kepler's laws come straight out of gravity and his laws of motion.

Did you know? Real planet orbits are very close to circles. Earth's is so round you couldn't tell it from a circle by eye; drawings like this one stretch it so the idea is easier to see.

20.text:
Check for Understanding: Find the Period

Your turn to use Kepler's third law. A planet orbits at 4 AU. How long does it take to go around the Sun once?

Is it A) 4 years, B) 8 years, C) 16 years, or D) 64 years? Write out P2 = a3, plug in the number, and watch each step. Every wrong answer is waiting for a common slip.

21.text:
Myth Check: The Seasons

Lots of people think summer happens because Earth gets closer to the Sun. Nope. Seasons are caused by Earth's 23.4° tilt, not its distance.

Here's the proof. Earth is closest to the Sun, about 147 million km away, in early January. That's the middle of winter in the Northern Hemisphere! In June, the north tilts toward the Sun. In December, the north tilts away.

When your half of Earth tilts toward the Sun, sunlight hits it more directly, like a flashlight pointed straight down instead of at a slant, and the days are longer. Both add up to more warmth. Tilt away, and the light spreads out and the days get short.

Did you know? When it's summer in the United States, it's winter in Australia. If distance caused seasons, the whole planet would have the same season at once.

22.text:
Activity: The Scale Walk

Remember the grapefruit Sun? Now we build the model for real, at a scale of 1 : 10 billion. On this scale, the Sun is 14 cm, a grapefruit, at the start. Earth is a 1.3 mm pinhead 15 m away. Jupiter is a 1.4 cm marble 78 m away. Neptune is a 5 mm peppercorn 450 m away.

Walk it out and feel the distances. Fifteen big steps to a pinhead you can barely see. Then a long walk to the marble, and a really long walk to the peppercorn. Notice what's in between: almost nothing. The solar system is mostly empty space.

And the next star? Alpha Centauri would be another grapefruit about 4,100 km away. Check that against the guess you made on Slide 2. How close did you get?

Did you know? Neptune at 450 m in this model is roughly the length of five football fields.

23.text:
Exit Ticket

You covered a lot of ground today. Show what you've got with three quick questions.

First, write Earth's cosmic address, 6 levels. Second, explain why looking far away is looking back in time. Third, fill in the blank: gravity at the ISS is about ___% of Earth's. Then explain why astronauts float.

When you're done, look back at your "I can" list from Slide 3 and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

24.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask you to do, in plain words.

ES.1.1: explain how we study space by observing all kinds of light, using different telescopes and tools. ES.1.5: show how stars, planetary systems (including multiple-star systems), star clusters, galaxies, and groups of galaxies fit inside one another, and how big each one is. ES.2.4: use math to describe how planets, moons, comets, and asteroids move, and explain that Kepler's laws come from Newton's law of gravity and his laws of motion.

Two more get a first introduction here and come back later. ES.1.2 is about the expanding universe, or Big Bang theory, and the evidence for it: the Doppler effect, redshift, Hubble's Law, and the cosmic microwave background. ES.2.5 is about how science changes as new observations come in, from the ancient Greek astronomer Ptolemy to Copernicus, Brahe, Kepler, and Galileo. You'll see the cosmology in a later quarter and the history in Deck 3.
